On January 20, 2007, Hillary Clinton, former first lady and then-Senator representing New York, announced that she would run for President of the United States.
Clinton sought the Democratic Party's 2008 nomination for president.
She campaigned with the slogan "Solutions for America!" and the chant "Yes We Will".
Although Clinton had strong support and won many primaries, she ultimately lost the nomination to Barack Obama, who was elected president on November 4, 2008.
Clinton suspended her campaign on June 7, 2008.
Hillary Clinton greets supporters after her New Hampshire Primary win.

Because of a party dispute over scheduling, the January 15 Michigan primary lost its delegates to the national convention, and all major candidates signed a pledge "not to campaign or participate" in Michigan's primary.
The majority of candidates, including Richardson, Edwards and Obama, interpreted the pledge as requiring the removal of their names from the Michigan ballot.
Clinton, however, decided to keep her name on the ballot, only agreeing to the "campaign" part of the pledge.

Thus, little or no campaigning was done there (in the actual vote, Clinton would win nothing with 55 percent of the vote against 40 percent for an uncommitted slate[126]) and attention instead moved to the January 19 Nevada caucuses.

Bill Clinton attracted controversy for his participation in his wife's campaign after a series of attacks made on his part against Obama, which many former Clinton supporters felt to be unfair.[149][150][151] While some felt the attacks against Obama may eventually pay off,[152] others felt it would damage Hillary Clinton's presidential prospects and alienate Democratic voters in the general election if she won the nomination.[149][153] There was also concern that the former president was overshadowing the candidate on the campaign trail.[154][155][156] According to CBS, "By injecting himself into the Democratic primary campaign with a series of inflammatory and negative statements, Bill Clinton may have helped his wife's presidential hopes in the long term but at the cost of his reputation with a group of voters that have long been one of his strongest bases of political support."[157][158] Some critics accused Clinton of "pulling the race card"[159][160][161] against Barack Obama.
Kennedy Jr.[165] and his sisters Kathleen Kennedy Townsend and Kerry Kennedy[166] (children of the late Senator and United States Attorney General, Robert F.
Kennedy) announced that they would be endorsing Hillary Clinton.
Bill Clinton campaigning for Hillary Clinton at Virginia Tech.
Clinton campaigning at Augsburg College in Minneapolis, Minnesota, two days before the twenty-two state vote.
The "Potomac primary", with votes cast in Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, was held on February 12.

With a week and a half to go, both Ohio and Texas tightened: An ABC News/Washington Post poll taken February 16–20 indicated that Clinton's lead over Obama in Ohio had shrunk to 7 percentage points.[259] Another poll, released February 25, projected also a statistical dead heat in Texas between the two.[260] On February 25 _USA Today_/Gallup poll showed that Obama had a double-digit lead for the first time,[261] and a CBS News/New York Times poll showed an even larger Obama lead.
On March 27, Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont called for Clinton to withdraw from the presidential campaign and support opponent Barack Obama.
The six-term senator, and chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee made the statements during an interview on Vermont Public Radio.
Leahy stated: "Senator Clinton has every right, but not a very good reason, to remain a candidate for as long as she wants to.

As far as the delegate count and the interests of a Democratic victory in November go, there is not a very good reason for drawing this out."[348] Clinton rejected calls to withdraw, saying "The more people get a chance to vote, the better it is for our democracy...we of all people [know] how important it [is] to give everyone a chance to have their voices heard and their votes counted." Campaigning in the week of April 14, 2008, included a tough debate between Obama and Clinton, who pounded her rival for his recent remark that decades of economic decline had left some rural voters "bitter" and clinging to religion and guns.
> ... people have been trying to push me out of this ever since Iowa and ...
I find it curious because it is unprecedented in history.

I don't understand it and between my opponent and his camp and some in the media, there has been this urgency to end this and you know historically that makes no sense, so I find it a bit of a mystery. ...
You know my husband did not wrap up the nomination in 1992 until he won the California primary somewhere around the middle of June ...
We all remember Bobby Kennedy was assassinated in June in California.
Um, you know I just I don't understand it.
There's lots of speculation about why it is.
On June 1, Clinton won the Puerto Rico primary by more than a 2-to-1 margin.[389] Later on June 3, Clinton won the South Dakota primary and Obama won the Montana primary.
This was the final primary of the season.

Following the result, after rumors fueled by a misunderstanding of an Associated Press report, the campaign dismissed suggestions that Clinton was going to concede in the speech following the primaries.[391] In her speech after the closing of the Montana polls, Clinton said "I will be making no decisions tonight."[392] She invited Americans to write to her on her website to provide input into what her next steps should be.
Clinton speaks during the second night of the 2008 Democratic National Convention in Denver, Colorado, while delegates and audience members hold signs reading "Hillary".
During the Democratic National Convention, Clinton released her delegates and urged them to vote for Barack Obama.
On August 27, 2008, she motioned that Sen.
Obama be officially nominated by acclamation.
